entries.a8fa9e87e15e1a5e4b4eb7bf36967ead67a57ab3: <div sID="gen5871" type="x-p"/> <chapter n="28" osisID="1Sam.28" sID="1Sam.28"/> <div eID="gen5871" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5872" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen5873" type="x-p"/> Preparations are herein making for that war which will put an end to the life and reign of Saul, and so make way for David to the throne. In this war, I. The Philistines are the aggressors and Achish their king makes David his confidant, <reference osisRef="1Sam.28.1-1Sam.28.2">ver. 1, 2</reference>. II. The Israelites prepare to receive them, and Saul their king makes the devil his privy-counsellor, and thereby fills the measure of his iniquity. Observe, 1. The despairing condition which Saul was in, <reference osisRef="1Sam.28.3-1Sam.28.6">ver. 3-6</reference>. 2. The application he made to a witch, to bring him up Samuel, <reference osisRef="1Sam.28.7-1Sam.28.14">ver. 7-14</reference>. 3. His discourse with the apparition, <reference osisRef="1Sam.28.15-1Sam.28.19">ver. 15-19</reference>. The damp it struck upon him, <reference osisRef="1Sam.28.20-1Sam.28.25">ver. 20-25</reference>.
entries.3e26a78548b863b94bef8863e9a9982889381b07: <div eID="gen5873" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen5872" type="introduction"/> <title type="x-s3">The Philistines Make War on Israel. (<hi type="small-caps">b. c.</hi> 1055.)</title> <div sID="gen5874" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">1</hi> And it came to pass in those days, that the Philistines gathered their armies together for warfare, to fight with Israel. And Achish said unto David, Know thou assuredly, that thou shalt go out with me to battle, thou and thy men. <hi type="super">2</hi> And David said to Achish, Surely thou shalt know what thy servant can do. And Achish said to David, Therefore will I make thee keeper of mine head for ever. <hi type="super">3</hi> Now Samuel was dead, and all Israel had lamented him, and buried him in Ramah, even in his own city. And Saul had put away those that had familiar spirits, and the wizards, out of the land. <hi type="super">4</hi> And the Philistines gathered themselves together, and came and pitched in Shunem: and Saul gathered all Israel together, and they pitched in Gilboa. <hi type="super">5</hi> And when Saul saw the host of the Philistines, he was afraid, and his heart greatly trembled. <hi type="super">6</hi> And when Saul enquired of the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> , the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> answered him not, neither by dreams, nor by Urim, nor by prophets. <div eID="gen5874" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5875" type="x-p"/> Here is, I. The design of the Philistines against Israel. They resolved to <hi type="italic">fight them,</hi> <reference osisRef="1Sam.28.1">v. 1</reference>. If the Israelites had not forsaken God, there would have been no Philistines remaining to molest them; if Saul had not forsaken him, they would by this time have been put out of all danger by them. The Philistines took an opportunity to make this attempt when they had David among them, whom they feared more than Saul and all his forces. <div eID="gen5875" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5876" type="x-p"/> II. The expectation Achish had of assistance from David in this war, and the encouragement David gave him to expect it: "<hi type="italic">Thou shalt go with me to battle,</hi>" says Achish. "If I protect thee, I may demand service from thee;" and he will think himself happy if he may have such a man as David on his side, who prospered whithersoever he went. David gave him an ambiguous answer: "We will see what will be done; it will be time enough to talk of that hereafter; but <hi type="italic">surely thou shalt know what thy servant can do</hi>" (<reference osisRef="1Sam.28.2">v. 2</reference>), that is, "I will consider in what post I may be best able to serve thee, if thou wilt but give me leave to choose it." Thus he keeps himself free from a promise to serve him and yet keeps up his expectation of it; for Achish took it in no other sense than as an engagement to assist him, and promised him, thereupon, that he would make him captain of the guards, protector, or prime-minister of state. <div eID="gen5876" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5877" type="x-p"/> III. The drawing of the armies, on both sides, into the field (<reference osisRef="1Sam.28.4">v. 4</reference>): <hi type="italic">The Philistines pitched in Shunem,</hi> which was in the tribe of Issachar, a great way north from their country. The land of Israel, it seems, was ill-guarded, when the Philistines could march their army into the very heart of the country. Saul, while he pursued David, left his people naked and exposed. On some of the adjacent mountains of Gilboa Saul mustered his forces, and prepared to engage the Philistines, which he had little heart to do now that the <hi type="italic">Spirit of the Lord had departed from him.</hi> <div eID="gen5877" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5878" type="x-p"/> IV. The terror Saul was in, and the loss he was at, upon this occasion: He <hi type="italic">saw the host of the Philistines,</hi> and by his own view of them, and the intelligence his spies brought him, he perceived they were more numerous, better armed, and in better heart, than his own were, which made him afraid, so that <hi type="italic">his heart greatly trembled,</hi> <reference osisRef="1Sam.28.5">v. 5</reference>. Had he kept close to God, he needed not have been afraid at the sight of an army of Philistines; but now that he had provoked God to forsake him his interest failed, his armies dwindled and looked mean, and, which was worse, his spirits failed him, his heart sunk within him, a guilty conscience made him tremble at the shaking of a leaf. Now he remembered the guilty blood of the Amalekites which he had spared, and the innocent blood of the priests which he had spilt. His sins were set in order before his eyes, which put him into confusion, embarrassed all his counsels, robbed him of all his courage, and produced in him a certain fearful looking for of judgment and fiery indignation. Note, Troubles are terrors to the children of disobedience. In this distress <hi type="italic">Saul enquired of the Lord,</hi> <reference osisRef="1Sam.28.6">v. 6</reference>. Need drives those to God who in the day of their prosperity slighted his oracles and altars. <hi type="italic">Lord, in trouble have they visited thee,</hi> <reference osisRef="Isa.26.16">Isa. xxvi. 16</reference>. Did ever any seek the Lord and not find him? Yes, Saul did; <hi type="italic">the Lord answered him not,</hi> took no notice either of his petitions or of his enquiries; gave him no directions what to do, nor any encouragement to hope that he would be with him. <hi type="italic">Should he be enquired of at all</hi> by such a one as Saul? <reference osisRef="Ezek.14.3">Ezek. xiv. 3</reference>. No, he could not expect an answer of peace, for, 1. He enquired in such a manner that it was as if he had <hi type="italic">not enquired at all.</hi> Therefore it is said (<reference osisRef="1Chr.10.14">1 Chron. x. 14</reference>), <hi type="italic">He enquired not of the Lord;</hi> for he did it faintly and coldly, and with a secret design, if God did not answer him, to consult the devil. He did not enquire in faith, but with a double unstable mind. 2. He enquired of the Lord when it was too late, when the days of his probation were over and he was finally rejected. <hi type="italic">Seek the Lord while he may be found,</hi> for there is a time when he will not be found. 3. He had forfeited the benefit of all the methods of enquiry. Could he that hated and persecuted Samuel and David, who were both prophets, expect to be answered by prophets? Could he that had slain the high priest, expect to be answered by Urim? Or could he that had sinned away the Spirit of grace, expect to be answered by dreams? No. <hi type="italic">Be not deceived, God is not mocked.</hi> <div eID="gen5878" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5879" type="x-p"/> V. The mention of some things that had happened a good while ago, to introduce the following story, <reference osisRef="1Sam.28.3">v. 3</reference>. 1. The death of Samuel. Samuel was dead, which made the Philistines the more bold and Saul the more afraid; for, had Samuel been alive, Saul probably thought that his presence and countenance, his good advice and good prayers, would have availed him in his distress. 2. Saul's edict against witchcraft. He had put the laws in execution against <hi type="italic">those that had familiar spirits,</hi> who must not be <hi type="italic">suffered to live,</hi> <reference osisRef="Exod.22.18">Exod. xxii. 18</reference>. Some think that he did this in the beginning of his reign, while he was under Samuel's influence; others think that it was lately done, for it is spoken of here (<reference osisRef="1Sam.28.9">v. 9</reference>) as a late edict. Perhaps when Saul was himself troubled with an evil spirit he suspected that he was bewitched, and, for that reason, cut off all that had familiar spirits. Many seem zealous against sin, when they themselves are any way hurt by it (they will inform against swearers if they swear at them, or against drunkards if in their drink they abuse them), who otherwise have no concern for the glory of God, nor any dislike of sin as sin. However it was commendable in Saul thus to use his power for the terror and restraint of these evil-doers. Note, Many seem enemies to sin in others, while they indulge it in themselves. Saul will drive the devil out of his kingdom, and yet harbour him in his heart, by envy and malice.
entries.33e639ea173c8783765236959ea0dd311c178691: <div eID="gen5879" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">Saul Consults the Witch at Endor. (<hi type="small-caps">b. c.</hi> 1055.)</title> <div sID="gen5880" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">7</hi> Then said Saul unto his servants, Seek me a woman that hath a familiar spirit, that I may go to her, and enquire of her. And his servants said to him, Behold, <hi type="italic">there is</hi> a woman that hath a familiar spirit at Endor. <hi type="super">8</hi> And Saul disguised himself, and put on other raiment, and he went, and two men with him, and they came to the woman by night: and he said, I pray thee, divine unto me by the familiar spirit, and bring me <hi type="italic">him</hi> up, whom I shall name unto thee. <hi type="super">9</hi> And the woman said unto him, Behold, thou knowest what Saul hath done, how he hath cut off those that have familiar spirits, and the wizards, out of the land: wherefore then layest thou a snare for my life, to cause me to die? <hi type="super">10</hi> And Saul sware to her by the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> , saying, <hi type="italic">As</hi> the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> liveth, there shall no punishment happen to thee for this thing. <hi type="super">11</hi> Then said the woman, Whom shall I bring up unto thee? And he said, Bring me up Samuel. <hi type="super">12</hi> And when the woman saw Samuel, she cried with a loud voice: and the woman spake to Saul, saying, Why hast thou deceived me? for thou <hi type="italic">art</hi> Saul. <hi type="super">13</hi> And the king said unto her, Be not afraid: for what sawest thou? And the woman said unto Saul, I saw gods ascending out of the earth. <hi type="super">14</hi> And he said unto her, What form <hi type="italic">is</hi> he of? And she said, An old man cometh up; and he <hi type="italic">is</hi> covered with a mantle. And Saul perceived that it <hi type="italic">was</hi> Samuel, and he stooped with <hi type="italic">his</hi> face to the ground, and bowed himself. <div eID="gen5880" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5881" type="x-p"/> Here, I. Saul seeks for a witch, <reference osisRef="1Sam.28.7">v. 7</reference>. When God <hi type="italic">answered him not,</hi> if he had humbled himself by repentance and persevered in seeking God, who knows but that at length he might have been entreated for him? but, since he can discern no comfort either from heaven or earth (<reference osisRef="Isa.8.21-Isa.8.22">Isa. viii. 21, 22</reference>), he resolves to knock at the gates of hell, and to see if any there will befriend him and give him advice: <hi type="italic">Seek me a woman that has a familiar spirit,</hi> <reference osisRef="1Sam.28.7">v. 7</reference>. And his servants were too officious to serve him in this evil affair; they presently recommended one to him at Endor (a city not far off) who had escaped the execution of Saul's edict. To her he resolves to apply. Herein he is chargeable, 1. With contempt of the God of Israel; as if any creature could do him a kindness when God had left him and frowned upon him. 2. With contradiction to himself. He knew the heinousness of the sin of witchcraft, else he would not have cut off those that had familiar spirits; yet now he had recourse to that as an oracle which he had before condemned as an abomination. It is common for men to inveigh severely against those sins which they are in no temptation to, but afterwards to be themselves overcome by them. Had one told Saul, when he was destroying the witches, that he himself would, ere long, consult with one, he would have said, as Hazael did, <hi type="italic">What? Is thy servant a dog?</hi> But who knows what mischiefs those will run into that forsake God and are forsaken of him? <div eID="gen5881" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5882" type="x-p"/> II. Hearing of one he hastens to her, but goes by night, and in disguise, only with two servants, and probably on foot, <reference osisRef="1Sam.28.8">v. 8</reference>. See how those that are led captive by Satan are forced, 1. To disparage themselves. Never did Saul look so mean as when he went sneaking to a sorry witch to know his fortune. 2. To dissemble. Evil works are works of darkness, and they hate the light, neither care for coming to it. Saul went to the witch, not in his robes, but in the habit of a common soldier, not only lest the witch herself, if she had known him, should decline to serve him, either fearing he came to trepan her or resolving to be avenged on him for his edict against those of her profession, but lest his own people should know it and abhor him for it. Such is the power of natural conscience that even those who do evil blush and are ashamed to do it. <div eID="gen5882" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5883" type="x-p"/> III. He tells her his errand and promises her impunity. 1. All he desires of her is to bring up one from the dead, whom he had a mind to discourse with. It was necromancy or divination by the dead, that he hoped to serve his purpose by. This was expressly forbidden by the law (<reference osisRef="Deut.18.11">Deut. xviii. 11</reference>), seeking <hi type="italic">for the living to the dead,</hi> <reference osisRef="Isa.8.19">Isa. viii. 19</reference>. <hi type="italic">Bring me up him whom I shall name,</hi> <reference osisRef="1Sam.28.8">v. 8</reference>. This supposes that it was generally taken for granted that souls exist after death, and that when men die there is not an end of them: it supposes too that great knowledge was attributed to separate souls. But to think that any good souls would come up at the beck of an evil spirit, or that God, who had denied a man the benefit of his own institutions, would suffer him to reap any real advantage by a cursed diabolical invention, was very absurd. 2. She signifies her fear of the law, and her suspicion that this stranger came to draw her into a snare (<reference osisRef="1Sam.28.9">v. 9</reference>): <hi type="italic">Thou knowest what Saul has done.</hi> Providence ordered it so that Saul should be told to his face of his edict against witches, at this very time when he was consulting one, for the greater aggravation of his sin. She insists upon the peril of the law, perhaps to raise her price; for, though no mention is made of her fee, no doubt she demanded and had a large one. Observe how sensible she is of danger from the edict of Saul, and what care she is in to guard against it; but not at all apprehensive of the obligations off God's law and the terrors of his wrath. She considered what <hi type="italic">Saul</hi> had done, not what <hi type="italic">God</hi> had done, against such practices, and feared a snare laid for her life more than a snare laid for her soul. It is common for sinners to be more afraid of punishment from men than of God's righteous judgment. But, 3. Saul promises with an oath not to betray her, <reference osisRef="1Sam.28.10">v. 10</reference>. It was his duty as a king to punish her and he knew it, yet he swears no to do it; as if he could by his own oath bind himself from doing that which, by the divine command, he was bound to do. But he promised more than he could perform when he said, <hi type="italic">There shall no punishment happen to thee;</hi> for he that could not secure himself could much less secure her from divine vengeance. <div eID="gen5883" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5884" type="x-p"/> IV. Samuel, who was lately dead, is the person whom Saul desired to have some talk with; and the witch, with her enchantments, gratifies his desire, and brings them together. 1. As soon as Saul had given the witch the assurance she desired (that he would not discover her) she applied to her witchcrafts, and asked very confidently, <hi type="italic">Whom shall I bring up to thee?</hi> <reference osisRef="1Sam.28.11">v. 11</reference>. Note, Hopes of impunity embolden sinners in their evil ways and harden their hearts. 2. Saul desires to speak with Samuel: <hi type="italic">Bring me up Samuel.</hi> Samuel had anointed him to the kingdom and had formerly been his faithful friend and counsellor, and therefore with him he wished to advise. While Samuel was living at Ramah, not far from Gibeah of Saul, and presided there in the school of the prophets, we never read of Saul's going to him to consult him in any of the difficulties he was in (it would have been well for him if he had); then he slighted him, and perhaps hated him, looking upon him to be in David's interest. But now that he is dead, "O for Samuel again! By all means, <hi type="italic">bring me up Samuel.</hi>" Note, Many that despise and persecute God's saints and ministers when they are living would be glad to have them again when they are gone. <hi type="italic">Send Lazarus to me,</hi> and <hi type="italic">send Lazarus to my father's house,</hi> <reference osisRef="Luke.16.24-Luke.16.27">Luke xvi. 24-27</reference>. The sepulchres of the righteous are garnished. 3. Here is a seeming defector chasm in the story. Saul said, <hi type="italic">Bring me up Samuel,</hi> and the very next words are, <hi type="italic">When the woman saw Samuel,</hi> (<reference osisRef="1Sam.28.12">v. 12</reference>), whereas one would have expected to be told how she performed the operation, what spells and charms she used, or that some little intimation would be given of what she said or did; but the profound silence of the scripture concerning it forbids our coveting to <hi type="italic">know the depths of Satan</hi> (<reference osisRef="Rev.2.24">Rev. ii. 24</reference>) or to have our curiosity gratified with an account of the mysteries of iniquity. It has been said of the books of some of the popish confessors that, by their descriptions of sin, they have taught men to commit it; but the scripture conceals sinful art, that we may be <hi type="italic">simple concerning evil,</hi> <reference osisRef="Rom.16.9">Rom. xvi. 19</reference>. 4. The witch, upon sight of the apparition, was aware that her client was Saul, her familiar spirit, it is likely, informing her of it (<reference osisRef="1Sam.28.12">v. 12</reference>): "<hi type="italic">Why hast thou deceived me</hi> with a disguise; for thou art Saul, the very man that I am afraid of above any man?" Thus she gave Saul to understand the power of her art, in that she could discover him through his disguise; and yet she feared lest, hereafter, at least, he should take advantage against her for what she was now doing. Had she believed that it was really Samuel whom she saw, she would have had more reason to be afraid of him, who was a good prophet, than of Saul, who was a wicked king. But the wrath of earthly princes is feared by most more than the wrath of the King of kings. 5. Saul (who, we may suppose, was kept at a distance in the next room) bade her not to be afraid of him, but go on with the operation, and enquired <hi type="italic">what she saw?</hi> <reference osisRef="1Sam.28.13">v. 13</reference>. <hi type="italic">O,</hi> says the woman, <hi type="italic">I saw gods</hi> (that is, a spirit) <hi type="italic">ascending out of the earth;</hi> they called angels <hi type="italic">gods,</hi> because spiritual beings. Poor gods that ascend <hi type="italic">out of the earth!</hi> But she speaks the language of the heathen, who had their infernal deities and had them in veneration. If Saul had thought it necessary to his conversation with Samuel that the body of Samuel should be called out of the grave, he would have taken the witch with him to Ramah, where his sepulchre was; but the design was wholly upon his soul, which yet, if it became visible, was expected to appear in the usual resemblance of the body; and God permitted the devil, to answer the design, to put on Samuel's shape, that those who would not <hi type="italic">receive the love of the truth</hi> might be <hi type="italic">given up to strong delusions and believe a lie.</hi> That it could not be the soul of Samuel himself they might easily apprehend when it <hi type="italic">ascended out of the earth,</hi> for the <hi type="italic">spirit of a man,</hi> much more of a good man, <hi type="italic">goes upward,</hi> <reference osisRef="Eccl.3.21">Eccl. iii. 21</reference>. But, if people will be deceived, it is just with God to say, "Let them be deceived." That the devil, by the divine permission, should be able to personate Samuel is not strange, since he can <hi type="italic">transform himself into an angel of light!</hi> nor is it strange that he should be permitted to do it upon this occasion, that Saul might be driven to despair, by enquiring of the devil, since he would not, in a right manner, enquire of the Lord, by which he might have had comfort. Saul, being told of gods ascending, was eager to know what was the form of this deity, and in what shape he appeared, so far was he from conceiving any horror at it, his heart being wretchedly <hi type="italic">hardened by the deceitfulness of sin.</hi> Saul, it seems, was not permitted to see any manner of similitude himself, but he must take the woman's word for it, that she saw <hi type="italic">an old man covered with a mantle, or robe,</hi> the habit of a judge, which Samuel had sometimes worn, and some think it was for the sake of that, and the majesty of its aspect, that she called this apparition <hi type="italic">Elohim, a god or gods;</hi> for so magistrates are styled, <reference osisRef="Ps.82.1">Ps. lxxxii. 1</reference>. 6. Saul, perceiving, by the woman's description, that it was Samuel, <hi type="italic">stooped with his face to the ground,</hi> either, as it is generally taken, in reverence to Samuel, though he saw him not, or perhaps to listen to that soft and muttering voice which he now expected to hear (for those that had familiar spirits <hi type="italic">peeped and muttered,</hi> <reference osisRef="Isa.8.19">Isa. viii. 19</reference>); and it should seem Saul bowed himself (probably by the witch's direction) that he might hear what was whispered and listen carefully to it; for the <hi type="italic">voice of one that has a familiar spirit</hi> is said to come <hi type="italic">out of the ground, and whisper out of the dust,</hi> <reference osisRef="Isa.29.4">Isa. xxix. 4</reference>. He would stoop to that who would not stoop to the word of God.
entries.5e626d9fcf130d8f757163ab3b21daaaabb41972: <div eID="gen5884" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">Saul's Death Foretold. (<hi type="small-caps">b. c.</hi> 1055.)</title> <div sID="gen5885" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">15</hi> And Samuel said to Saul, Why hast thou disquieted me, to bring me up? And Saul answered, I am sore distressed; for the Philistines make war against me, and God is departed from me, and answereth me no more, neither by prophets, nor by dreams: therefore I have called thee, that thou mayest make known unto me what I shall do. <hi type="super">16</hi> Then said Samuel, Wherefore then dost thou ask of me, seeing the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> is departed from thee, and is become thine enemy? <hi type="super">17</hi> And the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> hath done to him, as he spake by me: for the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> hath rent the kingdom out of thine hand, and given it to thy neighbour, <hi type="italic">even</hi> to David: <hi type="super">18</hi> Because thou obeyedst not the voice of the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> , nor executedst his fierce wrath upon Amalek, therefore hath the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> done this thing unto thee this day. <hi type="super">19</hi> Moreover the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> will also deliver Israel with thee into the hand of the Philistines: and to morrow <hi type="italic">shalt</hi> thou and thy sons <hi type="italic">be</hi> with me: the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> also shall deliver the host of Israel into the hand of the Philistines. <div eID="gen5885" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5886" type="x-p"/> We have here the conference between Saul and Satan. Saul came in disguise (<reference osisRef="1Sam.28.8">v. 8</reference>), but Satan soon discovered him, <reference osisRef="1Sam.28.12">v. 12</reference>. Satan comes in disguise, in the disguise of Samuel's mantle, and Saul cannot discover him. Such is the disadvantage we labour under, in wrestling with <hi type="italic">the rulers of the darkness of this world,</hi> that they know us, while we are ignorant of their wiles and devices. <div eID="gen5886" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5887" type="x-p"/> I. The spectre, or apparition, personating Samuel, asks why he is sent for (<reference osisRef="1Sam.28.15">v. 15</reference>): <hi type="italic">Why hast thou disquieted me to bring me up?</hi> To us this discovers that it was an evil spirit that personated Samuel; for (as bishop Patrick observes) it is not in the power of witches to disturb the rest of good men and to bring them back into the world when they please; nor would the true Samuel have acknowledged such a power in magical arts: but to Saul this was a proper device of Satan's, to draw veneration from him, to possess him with an opinion of the power of divination, and so to rivet him in the devil's interests. <div eID="gen5887" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5888" type="x-p"/> II. Saul makes his complaint to this counterfeit Samuel, mistaking him for the true; and a most doleful complaint it is: "<hi type="italic">I am sorely distressed,</hi> and know not what to do, <hi type="italic">for the Philistines make war against me;</hi> yet I should do well enough with them if I had but the tokens of God's presence with me; but, alas! <hi type="italic">God has departed from me.</hi>" He complained not of God's withdrawings till he fell into trouble, till the <hi type="italic">Philistines made war against him,</hi> and then he began to lament God's departure. He that in his prosperity enquired not after God in his adversity thought it hard that God answered him not, nor took any notice of his enquiries, either by dreams or prophets, neither gave answers immediately himself nor sent them by any of his messengers. He does not, like a penitent, own the righteousness of God in this; but, like a man enraged, flies out against God as unkind and flies off from him: <hi type="italic">Therefore I have called thee;</hi> as if Samuel, a servant of God, would favour those whom God frowned upon, or as if a dead prophet could do him more service than the living ones. One would think, from this, that he really desired to meet with the devil, and expected no other (though under the covert of Samuel's name), for he desires advice otherwise than from God, therefore from the devil, who is a rival with God. "God denies me, <hi type="italic">therefore I come to thee. Flectere si nequeo superos, Acheronta movebo.</hi>"—<hi type="italic">If I fail with heaven, I will move hell.</hi> <div eID="gen5888" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5889" type="x-p"/> III. It is cold comfort which this evil spirit in Samuel's mantle gives to Saul, and is manifestly intended to drive him to despair and self-murder. Had it been the true Samuel, when Saul desired to be told what he should do he would have told him to repent and make his peace with God, and recall David from his banishment, and would then have told him that he might hope in this way to find mercy with God; but, instead of that, he represents his case as helpless and hopeless, serving him as he did Judas, to whom he was first a tempter and then a tormentor, persuading him first to sell his master and then to hang himself. 1. He upbraids him with his present distress (<reference osisRef="1Sam.28.16">v. 16</reference>), tells him, not only that God had departed from him, but that he had become his enemy, and therefore he must expect no comfortable answer from him: "<hi type="italic">Wherefore dost thou ask me?</hi> How can I be thy friend when God is thy enemy, or thy counsellor when he has left thee?" 2. He upbraids him with the anointing of David to the kingdom, <reference osisRef="1Sam.28.17">v. 17</reference>. He could not have touched upon a string that sounded more unpleasant in the ear of Saul than this. Nothing is said to reconcile him to David, but all tends rather to exasperate him against David and widen the breach. Yet, to make him believe that he was Samuel, the apparition affirmed that it was God who spoke by him. The devil knows how to speak with an air of religion, and can teach <hi type="italic">false apostles to transform themselves into the apostles of Christ</hi> and imitate their language. Those who use spells and charms, and plead, in defence of them, that they find nothing in them but what is good, may remember what good words the devil here spoke, and yet with what a malicious design. 3. He upbraids him with his disobedience to the command of God in not destroying the Amalekites, <reference osisRef="1Sam.28.18">v. 18</reference>. Satan had helped him to palliate and excuse that sin when Samuel was dealing with him to bring him to repentance, but now he aggravates it, to make him despair of God's mercy. See what those get that hearken to Satan's temptations. He himself will be their accuser, and insult over them. And see whom those resemble that allure others to that which is evil and reproach them for it when they have done. 4. He foretels his approaching ruin, <reference osisRef="1Sam.28.19">v. 19</reference>. (1.) That his army should be routed by the Philistines. This is twice mentioned: <hi type="italic">The Lord shall deliver Israel into the hand of the Philistines.</hi> This he might foresee, by considering the superior strength and number of the Philistines, the weakness of the armies of Israel, Saul's terror, and especially God's departure from them. Yet, to personate a prophet, he very gravely ascribes it once and again to God: <hi type="italic">The Lord shall do it.</hi> (2.) That he and his sons should be slain in the battle: <hi type="italic">To-morrow,</hi> that is, in a little time (and, supposing that it was now after midnight, I see not but it may be taken strictly for the very next day after that which had now begun), <hi type="italic">thou and thy sons shall be with me,</hi> that is, in the state of the dead, separate from the body. Had this been the true Samuel, he could not have foretold the event unless God had revealed it to him; and, though it were an evil spirit, God might by him foretel it; as we read of an evil spirit that foresaw Ahab's fall at Ramoth-Gilead and was instrumental in it (<reference osisRef="1Kgs.22.20-1Kgs.22.23">1 Kings xxii. 20</reference>, &c.), as perhaps this evil spirit was, by the divine permission, in Saul's destruction. That evil spirit flattered Ahab, this frightened Saul, and both that they might fall; so miserable are those that are under the power of Satan; for, <hi type="italic">whether he rage or laugh, there is no rest,</hi> <reference osisRef="Prov.29.9">Prov. xxix. 9</reference>.
entries.ce9e46506a7561557fdc0b57b0d7f753966e4832: <div eID="gen5889" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">Saul's Despair. (<hi type="small-caps">b. c.</hi> 1055.)</title> <div sID="gen5890" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">20</hi> Then Saul fell straightway all along on the earth, and was sore afraid, because of the words of Samuel: and there was no strength in him; for he had eaten no bread all the day, nor all the night. <hi type="super">21</hi> And the woman came unto Saul, and saw that he was sore troubled, and said unto him, Behold, thine handmaid hath obeyed thy voice, and I have put my life in my hand, and have hearkened unto thy words which thou spakest unto me. <hi type="super">22</hi> Now therefore, I pray thee, hearken thou also unto the voice of thine handmaid, and let me set a morsel of bread before thee; and eat, that thou mayest have strength, when thou goest on thy way. <hi type="super">23</hi> But he refused, and said, I will not eat. But his servants, together with the woman, compelled him; and he hearkened unto their voice. So he arose from the earth, and sat upon the bed. <hi type="super">24</hi> And the woman had a fat calf in the house; and she hasted, and killed it, and took flour, and kneaded <hi type="italic">it,</hi> and did bake unleavened bread thereof: <hi type="super">25</hi> And she brought <hi type="italic">it</hi> before Saul, and before his servants; and they did eat. Then they rose up, and went away that night. <div eID="gen5890" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5891" type="x-p"/> We are here told how Saul received this terrible message from the ghost he consulted. He desired to be told <hi type="italic">what he should do</hi> (<reference osisRef="1Sam.28.15">v. 15</reference>), but was only told what he had not done and what should be done to him. Those that expect any good counsel or comfort otherwise than from God, and in the way of his institutions, will be as wretchedly disappointed as Saul here was. Observe, <div eID="gen5891" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5892" type="x-p"/> I. How he sunk under the load, <reference osisRef="1Sam.28.20">v. 20</reference>. He was indeed unfit to bear it, having <hi type="italic">eaten nothing all the day</hi> before, nor <hi type="italic">that night.</hi> He came fasting from the camp, and continued fasting; not for want of food, but for want of an appetite. The fear he was in of the power of the Philistines (<reference osisRef="1Sam.28.5">v. 5</reference>) took away his appetite, or perhaps the struggle he had with his own conscience, after he had entertained the thought of consulting the witch, made him to nauseate even his necessary food, though ever so dainty. This made him an easy prey to this fresh terror that now came upon him like an armed man. <hi type="italic">He fell all along on the earth,</hi> as if the archers of the Philistines had already hit him, <hi type="italic">and there was no strength in him</hi> to bear up against these heavy tidings. Now he had enough of consulting witches, and found them miserable comforters. When God in his word speaks terror to sinners he opens to them, at the same time, a door of hope if they repent: but those that apply to the gates of hell for succour must there expect darkness without any glimpse of light. <div eID="gen5892" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5893" type="x-p"/> II. With what difficulty he was persuaded to take so much relief as was necessary to carry him back to his post in the camp. The witch, it should seem, had left Saul alone with the spectre, to have his talk with him by himself; but perhaps hearing him fall and groan, and perceiving him to be in great agony, she came to him (<reference osisRef="1Sam.28.21">v. 21</reference>), and was very importunate with him to take some refreshment, that he might be able to get clear from her house, fearing that if he should be ill, especially if he should die there, she should be punished for it as a traitor, though she had escaped punishment as a witch. This, it is probable, rather than any sentiment of kindness, made her solicitous to help him. But what a deplorable condition had he brought himself to when he needed so wretched a comforter! 1. She showed herself very importunate with him to take some refreshment. She pleaded (<reference osisRef="1Sam.28.21">v. 21</reference>) that she had obeyed his voice to the endangering of her life, and why therefore should not he hearken to her voice for the relieving of his life? <reference osisRef="1Sam.28.22">v. 22</reference>. She had a fat calf at hand (and the word signifies one that was made use of in treading out the corn, and therefore could the worse be spared); this she prepared for his entertainment, <reference osisRef="1Sam.28.24">v. 24</reference>. Josephus is large in applauding the extraordinary courtesy and liberality of this woman, and recommending what she did as an example of compassion to the distressed, and readiness to communicate for their relief, though we have no prospect of being recompensed. 2. He showed himself very averse to it: <hi type="italic">He refused, and said, I will not eat</hi> (<reference osisRef="1Sam.28.23">v. 23</reference>), choosing rather to die obscurely by famine than honourably by the sword. Had he laboured only under a defect of animal spirits, food might have helped him; but, alas! his case was out of the reach of such succours. What are dainty meats to a wounded conscience? <hi type="italic">As vinegar upon nitre, so is he that sings songs to a heavy heart,</hi> so disagreeable and unwelcome. 3. The woman at length, with the help of his servants, overpersuaded him, against his inclination and resolution, to take some refreshment. Not by force, but by friendly advice, they <hi type="italic">compelled him</hi> (<reference osisRef="1Sam.28.23">v. 23</reference>), and of no other than such a rational and courteous compulsion are we to understand that in the parable, <hi type="italic">Compel them to come in,</hi> <reference osisRef="Luke.14.23">Luke xiv. 23</reference>. <hi type="italic">How forcible are right words,</hi> when men are pressed by them to that which is for their own interest! <reference osisRef="Job.6.25">Job vi. 25</reference>. Saul was somewhat revived with this entertainment; so that he and his servants, when they had eaten, <hi type="italic">rose up and went away</hi> before it was light (<reference osisRef="1Sam.28.25">v. 25</reference>), that they might hasten to their business and that they might not be seen to come out of such a scandalous house. Josephus here much admires the bravery and magnanimity of Saul, that, though he was assured he should lose both his life and honour, yet he would not desert his army, but resolutely returned to the camp, and stood ready for an engagement. I wonder more at the hardness of his heart, that he did not again apply to God by repentance and prayer, in hopes yet to obtain at least a reprieve; but he desperately ran headlong upon his own ruin. Perhaps, indeed, now that rage and envy possessed him to the uttermost, he was the better reconciled to his hard fate, being told that his sons, and Jonathan among the rest, whom he hated for his affection to David, should die with him. If he must fall, he cared not what desolations of his family and kingdom accompanied his fall, hoping it would be the worse for his successor. <hi type="bold"><hi type="italic">Emou thanontos gaia michtheto pyri.</hi></hi>—<hi type="italic">I care not if, when I am dead, the world should be set on fire.</hi> He begged not, as David, "Let thy hand be against me, but not against thy people."  <chapter eID="1Sam.28"/> <div eID="gen5893" type="x-p"/>

entries.974df5662aae9e5f4fb9a71ab39b60c1fa6c8fff: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv2793"/><title type="x-s2">CHAPTER 28</title> <div sID="gen3829" type="x-p"/> <reference osisRef="1Sam.28.1-1Sam.28.6">1Sa 28:1-6</reference>. Achish's Confidence in David.<div eID="gen3829" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3830" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv2793"/><hi type="bold">1. The Philistines gathered their armies together for warfare, to fight with Israel--</hi>The death of Samuel, the general dissatisfaction with Saul, and the absence of David, instigated the cupidity of those restless enemies of Israel.<div eID="gen3830" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3831" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">Achish said to David, Know thou assuredly, that thou shalt go out with me to battle--</hi>This was evidently to try him. Achish, however, seems to have thought he had gained the confidence of David and had a claim on his services. <div eID="gen3831" type="x-p"/>
entries.a9b975494ddacd039dd959ee70b9c3967bdf563a: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv2794"/><div sID="gen3832" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv2794"/><hi type="bold">2. Surely thou shalt know what thy servant can do--</hi>This answer, while it seemed to express an apparent cheerfulness in agreeing to the proposal, contained a studied ambiguity--a wary and politic generality.<div eID="gen3832" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3833" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">Therefore will I make thee keeper of mine head for ever--</hi>or, "my life"; that is, "captain of my bodyguard," an office of great trust and high honor. <div eID="gen3833" type="x-p"/>
entries.4fa77a2ea3b2cda440cff063fc288937742d2025: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv2795"/><div sID="gen3834" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv2795"/><hi type="bold">3. Now Samuel is dead, &c.--</hi>This event is here alluded to as affording an explanation of the secret and improper methods by which Saul sought information and direction in the present crisis of his affairs. Overwhelmed in perplexity and fear, he yet found the common and legitimate channels of communication with Heaven shut against him. And so, under the impulse of that dark, distempered, superstitious spirit which had overmastered him, he resolved, in desperation, to seek the aid of one of those fortune telling impostors whom, in accordance with the divine command (<reference osisRef="Lev.19.31">Le 19:31</reference>; <reference osisRef="Lev.20.6">20:6</reference>, <reference osisRef="Lev.20.27">27</reference>; <reference osisRef="Deut.18.11">De 18:11</reference>), he had set himself formerly to exterminate from his kingdom. <div eID="gen3834" type="x-p"/>
entries.53a976a8ac3e99ebad06778c44d5b858fc0dc701: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv2796"/><div sID="gen3835" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv2796"/><hi type="bold">4. the Philistines ... pitched in Shunem--</hi>Having collected their forces for a last grand effort, they marched up from the seacoast and encamped in the "valley of Jezreel." The spot on which their encampment was fixed was Shunem (<reference osisRef="Josh.19.18">Jos 19:18</reference>), now Sulem, a village which still exists on the slope of a range called "Little Hermon." On the opposite side, on the rise of Mount Gilboa, hard by "the spring of Jezreel," was Saul's army--the Israelites, according to their wont, keeping to the heights, while their enemies clung to the plain.<div eID="gen3835" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3836" type="x-p"/> <reference osisRef="1Sam.28.7-1Sam.28.25">1Sa 28:7-25</reference>. Saul Seeks a Witch, Who, Being Encouraged by Him, Raises Up Samuel. <div eID="gen3836" type="x-p"/>
entries.d825f089b9b6465b9087f310da391ebd738822d2: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv2797"/><div sID="gen3837" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv2797"/><hi type="bold">7-8. Then said Saul unto his servants, Seek me a woman that hath a familiar spirit--</hi>From the energetic measures which he himself had taken for extirpating the dealers in magical arts (the profession having been declared a capital offense), his most attached courtiers might have had reason to doubt the possibility of gratifying their master's wish. Anxious inquiries, however, led to the discovery of a woman living very secluded in the neighborhood, who had the credit of possessing the forbidden powers. To her house he repaired by night in disguise, accompanied by two faithful servants.<div eID="gen3837" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3838" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">En-dor--</hi>"the fountain of the circle" (that figure being constantly affected by magicians) was situated directly on the other side of the Gilboa range, opposite Tabor; so that, in this midnight adventure, Saul had to pass over the shoulder of the ridge on which the Philistines were encamped. <div eID="gen3838" type="x-p"/>
entries.8ef264ce588396a9fe0dd1380049009dabf41ab2: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv2799"/><div sID="gen3840" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv2799"/><hi type="bold">24. the woman had a fat calf ... and she hasted, and killed it, &c.--</hi>(See on <reference osisRef="Gen.18.1-Gen.18.8">Ge 18:1-8</reference>). <div eID="gen3840" type="x-p"/>
entries.84287a4f628a973c09c85dd513d735f1c0cc3db0: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv2800"/><div sID="gen3841" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv2800"/><hi type="bold">25. Then they rose up, and went away that night--</hi>Exhausted by long abstinence, overwhelmed with mental distress, and now driven to despair, the cold sweat broke on his anxious brow, and he sank helpless on the ground. But the kind attentions of the woman and his servants having revived him, he returned to the camp to await his doom. <chapter eID="1Sam.28"/>

entries.a9340ca391309baa077222d9b14e339f7ad399f7: <div eID="gen10493" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s">Introduction</title> <div sID="gen10494" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen10495" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen10495" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen10494" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen10496" type="x-p"/> The Philistines prepare to attack the Israelites, and Achish informs David that he shall accompany him to battle, <reference osisRef="1Sam.28.1">1Sam 28:1</reference>, <reference osisRef="1Sam.28.2">1Sam 28:2</reference>. Saul, unable to obtain any answer from God, applies to a witch at En-dor to bring up Samuel that he may converse with him on the issue of the war, <reference osisRef="1Sam.28.3-1Sam.28.11">1Sam 28:3-11</reference>. Samuel appears, <reference osisRef="1Sam.28.12-1Sam.28.14">1Sam 28:12-14</reference>. He reproaches Saul with his misconduct, and informs him of his approaching ruin, <reference osisRef="1Sam.28.15-1Sam.28.19">1Sam 28:15-19</reference>. He is greatly distressed; but at the solicitations of the woman and his own servants, he takes some food, and departs the same night, <reference osisRef="1Sam.28.20-1Sam.28.25">1Sam 28:20-25</reference>. <div eID="gen10496" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10497" type="x-p"/> <hi type="bold">Verse 1</hi> <div eID="gen10497" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10498" type="x-p"/> The Philistines gathered their armies together - Sir Isaac Newton conjectures that the Philistines had got a great increase to their armies by vast numbers of men which Amasis had driven out of Egypt. This, with Samuel's death, and David's disgrace, were no inconsiderable motives to a new war, front which the Philistines had now every thing to hope. <div eID="gen10498" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10499" type="x-p"/> Thou shalt go out with me to battle - This he said, being deceived by what David had told him.
entries.524a0a40a6fd76d82f9bd76536c496d89b05e31a: <hi type="bold">Verse 2</hi> <div eID="gen10499" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10500" type="x-p"/> Surely thou shalt know what thy servant can do - This was another equivocal answer; and could only be understood by his succeeding conduct. It might imply what he could do in favor of the Philistines against Israel; or in favor of Israel against the Philistines. Achish understood it in the former sense; and therefore he said to David, I will make thee keeper of my head for ever; i.e., Thou shalt be captain of my life-guards.
entries.db224a4325f7da6cfe4675f972ae956036366c26: <hi type="bold">Verse 3</hi> <div eID="gen10500" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10501" type="x-p"/> Samuel was dead - And there was no longer a public accredited prophet to consult. <div eID="gen10501" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10502" type="x-p"/> Those that had familiar spirits, and the wizards - See the note on <reference osisRef="Lev.19.31">Lev 19:31</reference>, and <reference osisRef="Exo.22.18">Exo 22:18</reference>.
entries.b03ab1940598055015410d4556965ba2d7b034ba: <hi type="bold">Verse 5</hi> <div eID="gen10502" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10503" type="x-p"/> When Saul saw - He saw from the superiority of his enemies, from the state of his army, and especially from his own state towards God, that he had every thing to fear.
entries.452998bc4204039feaf2eba670c50885e3a7f732: <hi type="bold">Verse 6</hi> <div eID="gen10503" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10504" type="x-p"/> The Lord answered him not - He used the three methods by which supernatural intelligence was ordinarily given: - <div eID="gen10504" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10505" type="x-p"/> 1. Dreams. - The person prayed for instruction; and begged that God would answer by a significant dream. <div eID="gen10505" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10506" type="x-p"/> 2. Urim. - This was a kind of oracular answer given to the high priest when clothed with the ephod, on which were the Urim and Thummim. How these communicated the answer, is not well known. <div eID="gen10506" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10507" type="x-p"/> 3. Prophets. - Who were requested by the party concerned to consult the Lord on the subject in question, and to report his answer. The prophets at that time could only be those in the schools of the prophets, which Samuel had established at Naioth and Gibeah. These were the only successors of Samuel that we know of.
entries.2ebd94265ca053628a20a7fef219aef260a88af4: <hi type="bold">Verse 7</hi> <div eID="gen10507" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10508" type="x-p"/> Seek me a woman that hath a familiar spirit - Literally, Seek me a woman, בעלת אוב baalath ob, the mistress of the Obidiah or Pythonic spirit - one who had a familiar spirit, whom she could invoke when she pleased, and receive answers from him relative to futurity. <div eID="gen10508" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10509" type="x-p"/> Strange that a man, who had banished all such from the land, as dangerous to the state, as impostors and deceivers, should now have recourse to them as the only persons in whom he could safely put his confidence in the time in which Jehovah had refused to help him! <div eID="gen10509" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10510" type="x-p"/> At En-dor - This was a city in the valley of Jezreel, at the foot of Mount Gilboa, where the army of Saul had now encamped.
entries.bfd0d5a35221a07c9051b18efeff9eb4557d37ea: <hi type="bold">Verse 8</hi> <div eID="gen10510" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10511" type="x-p"/> Saul disguised himself - That he might not be known by the woman, lest she, being terrified, should refuse to use her art.
entries.5ebe81006913efc8f0e131da33d5abcbc00afbcb: <hi type="bold">Verse 11</hi> <div eID="gen10511" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10512" type="x-p"/> Whom shall I bring up - The woman certainly meant no more than making her familiar personify whomsoever the querist should wish. In the evocation of spirits this is all that, according to the professed rules of their art, such persons pretend to; for over human souls in paradise or in the infernal regions they have no power. If we allow that there is such an art founded on true principles, all it can pretend to is, to bring up the familiar; cause him when necessary to assume the form and character of some particular person, and to give such notices relative to futurity as he is able to collect. And this even in the cases to which authenticity is generally allowed, is often scanty, vague, and uncertain, for fallen spirits do not abound in knowledge: this is an attribute of God, and rays of this perfection are imparted to pure and holy intelligences; and even Satan himself, as may be seen from most of his temptations, is far from excelling in knowledge. He may be cunning and insidious, but he certainly is not wise and prudent; we in general give this fallen spirit credit for much more wisdom than he possesses.
entries.e24340bf5850b54d4c958f9a54389d47344cf0cd: <hi type="bold">Verse 12</hi> <div eID="gen10512" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10513" type="x-p"/> When the woman saw Samuel - That Samuel did appear on this occasion, is most evident from the text; nor can this be denied from any legitimate mode of interpretation: and it is as evident that he was neither raised by the power of the devil nor the incantations of the witch, for the appearances which took place at this time were such as she was wholly unacquainted with. Her familiar did not appear; and from the confused description she gives, it is fully evident that she was both surprised and alarmed at what she saw, being so widely different from what she expected to see.
entries.4a85d110af0783c1047cb07b80aa3006e6a77685: <hi type="bold">Verse 13</hi> <div eID="gen10513" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10514" type="x-p"/> I saw gods ascending out of the earth - The word אלהום elohim, which we translate gods, is the word which is used for the Supreme Being throughout the Bible; but all the versions, the Chaldee excepted, translate it in the plural number, as we do. The Chaldee has, I see מלאכא דיי malacha dayeya, an angel of the Lord, ascending from the earth. This sight alarmed the woman; it was what she did not expect; in this she could not recognise her familiar, and she was terrified at the appearance.
entries.bf2e8c4ef06efe60f4db8bfac279213ee9f8968f: <hi type="bold">Verse 14</hi> <div eID="gen10514" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10515" type="x-p"/> An old man cometh up, and he is covered with a mantle - This seems to have been a second apparition; she cannot mean that she had seen gods ascending out of the earth, and these gods were like an old man with a mantle. The angelic appearance first mentioned prepared the way for Samuel; and the whole was done so as to show to the woman that her art had not prevailed in the present instance, and that what was now taking place was wholly independent of her incantations. <div eID="gen10515" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10516" type="x-p"/> Saul perceived that it was Samuel - The description was suitable to his person and clothing.
entries.21e097eb134f187e970aa1ee9be5acf794b6a4c0: <hi type="bold">Verse 15</hi> <div eID="gen10516" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10517" type="x-p"/> Why hast thou disquieted me - The complaint is not directed against the woman but against Saul. Indeed, her incantations had no influence in the business, and it does not appear that she had commenced her operations before the angels had prepared the way of the prophet, and before the prophet himself had made his appearance. <div eID="gen10517" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10518" type="x-p"/> That thou mayest make known unto me what I shall do - In his former difficulties, and when pressed by his enemies, he was in the habit of consulting Samuel; and now he applies to him as his former preceptor. God, he knew, might answer by such a man as Samuel, when he would answer by no other means.
entries.32c5f9af8eb8137459dc491b6bb36b837c7c93ab: <hi type="bold">Verse 16</hi> <div eID="gen10518" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10519" type="x-p"/> Wherefore then dost thou ask of me - Was ever I wont to give answers that were not dictated by the Lord? It is his counsel alone that I communicate.
entries.6a875b5d82d60cc2b7faf974aa82a346a33dd403: <hi type="bold">Verse 17</hi> <div eID="gen10519" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10520" type="x-p"/> The Lord hath done to him - I believe these words are spoken of Saul; and as they are spoken to him, it seems evident that him should be thee. The Vulgate has tibi, the Septuagint σοι, to Thee: and this is the reading of five of Kennicott's and De Rossi's MSS., as well as of both the Bibles printed at Venice in 1518, where we read לך lecha, to Thee, instead of לו lo, to Him. <div eID="gen10520" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10521" type="x-p"/> As he spake by me - Here was no illusion; none but Samuel could say this.
entries.f3f3ed15ff512ee90d976e9c96d0963c802b81bd: <hi type="bold">Verse 18</hi> <div eID="gen10521" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10522" type="x-p"/> Nor executedst his fierce wrath upon Amalek - See <reference osisRef="1Sam.15.1-1Sam.15.9">1Sam 15:1-9</reference> (note) and the notes there.
entries.8e9f8ac797942f619449e789aff4d39ae7d8963d: <hi type="bold">Verse 19</hi> <div eID="gen10522" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10523" type="x-p"/> To-morrow shalt thou and thy sons be with me - What an awful message! In the course of the ensuing day thou shalt be slain, thy three sons shall be slain, and the armies of Israel shall be delivered into the hands of the Philistines! Can any person read this, properly considering the situation of this unfortunate monarch, the triumph of the enemies of God, and the speedy ruin in which the godlike Jonathan is about to be involved, without feeling the keenest anguish of heart? <div eID="gen10523" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10524" type="x-p"/> But Samuel says, "He and his sons should be with him." Does not this mean that they were to go to paradise? I suppose it means no more than that they should all die. Yet the paraphrase of the Rev. C. Wesley is beautiful: - "What do these solemn words portend? <div eID="gen10524" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10525" type="x-p"/> A ray of hope when life shall end. <div eID="gen10525" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10526" type="x-p"/> Thou and thy sons, though slain, shall be <div eID="gen10526" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10527" type="x-p"/> To-morrow in repose with me. <div eID="gen10527" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10528" type="x-p"/> Not in a state of hellish pain, <div eID="gen10528" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10529" type="x-p"/> If Saul with Samuel do remain: <div eID="gen10529" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10530" type="x-p"/> Not in a state of damn'd despair, <div eID="gen10530" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10531" type="x-p"/> If loving Jonathan be there." <div eID="gen10531" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10532" type="x-p"/> Saul had committed the sin unto death - the sin to be visited with a violent death, while tile mercy of God was extended to the soul. Thus say my faith, my hope, and my charity; and doth not the mercy of God say the same?
entries.46d89b07de439ebae77706e8a83db850cac595af: <hi type="bold">Verse 20</hi> <div eID="gen10532" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10533" type="x-p"/> Then Saul fell straightway all along on the earth - Literally, he fell with his own length, or with the fullness of his stature. He was so overwhelmed with this most dreadful message, that he swooned away, and thus fell at his own length upon the ground. The woman, being terrified, had probably withdrawn to some distance at the first appearance of the prophet; and Saul was left alone with Samuel. After some short time, the woman came again unto Saul, found him sore troubled, and offered him those succours which humanity dictated.
entries.07ea0b47671e3247778ebc094656a8f1f07aa4b4: <hi type="bold">Verse 23</hi> <div eID="gen10533" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10534" type="x-p"/> I will not eat - It is no wonder that not only his strength, but also his appetite, had departed from him. <div eID="gen10534" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10535" type="x-p"/> And sat upon the bed - Beds or couches were the common places on which the ancients sat to take their repasts.
entries.5f97b6dbdb74948091f5a1ca42fdd1b6a8909340: <hi type="bold">Verse 24</hi> <div eID="gen10535" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10536" type="x-p"/> The woman had a fat calf - The ancients used great despatch in their cookery. In hot countries they could not keep flesh meat by them any length of time; hence they generally kept young animals, such as calves, lambs, and kids, ready for slaughter; and when there was occasion, one of them was killed, and dressed immediately. <div eID="gen10536" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10537" type="x-p"/> Unleavened bread - There was not time to bake leavened bread; that would have taken considerable time, in order that the leaven might leaven the whole lump.
entries.b764bee721b84f1bb511c9105708d20b18d29c9f: <hi type="bold">Verse 25</hi> <div eID="gen10537" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10538" type="x-p"/> They rose up, and went away that night - The transactions of this chapter occupy one night only. <div eID="gen10538" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10539" type="x-p"/> 1. Saul came by night to En-dor, <reference osisRef="1Sam.28.8">1Sam 28:8</reference>. <div eID="gen10539" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10540" type="x-p"/> 2. He consulted the woman, and had his conference with Samuel the same night; for no time whatever appears to have been lost after his arrival at En-dor. <div eID="gen10540" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10541" type="x-p"/> 3. He was overcome by the heavy tidings which he heard; and which for a time appear to have deprived him of all power. <div eID="gen10541" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10542" type="x-p"/> 4. The woman kills a calf; dresses a part; makes and bakes bread; and Saul and his servants eat. And, <div eID="gen10542" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10543" type="x-p"/> 5. They rose and went away that night, <reference osisRef="1Sam.28.25">1Sam 28:25</reference>. The next day, in all probability, the battle happened in which Israel was defeated, and Saul and his sons lost their lives. <div eID="gen10543" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10544" type="x-p"/> There is a considerable diversity of opinion, both among learned and pious men, relative to the subject mentioned in this chapter, that of raising Samuel from the dead. Some deny the possibility of the thing, and say that it was the devil that personified Samuel; and others, that the whole was the imposition of this cunning woman, and that there was no supernatural agency in the business. This is not a proper place to argue the point. I have given my opinion in the notes. I may sum up in a few particulars. <div eID="gen10544" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10545" type="x-p"/> 1. I believe there is a supernatural and spiritual world, in which Human spirits, both good and bad, live in a state of consciousness. <div eID="gen10545" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10546" type="x-p"/> 2. I believe there is an invisible world, in which various orders of spirits, not human, live and act. <div eID="gen10546" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10547" type="x-p"/> 3. I believe that any of these spirits may, according to the order of God, in the laws of their place of residence, have intercourse with this world, and become visible to mortals. <div eID="gen10547" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10548" type="x-p"/> 4. I believe there is a possibility, by arts not strictly good, to evoke and have intercourse with spirits, not Human; and to employ, in a certain limited way, their power and influence. <div eID="gen10548" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10549" type="x-p"/> 5. I believe that the woman of En-dor had no power over Samuel; and that no incantation can avail over any departed saint of God, nor indeed over any human disembodied spirit. <div eID="gen10549" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10550" type="x-p"/> 6. I believe Samuel did actually appear to Saul; and that he was sent by the especial mercy of God to warn this infatuated king of his approaching death, that he might have an opportunity to make his peace with his Maker. <div eID="gen10550" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10551" type="x-p"/> 7. I believe that the woman found, from the appearances, that her real or pretended charms had no effect; and that what now took place came from a totally different disposition of things from those with which she was conversant. <div eID="gen10551" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10552" type="x-p"/> 8. I believe that direct, circumstantial, and unequivocal oracles were now delivered concerning things which neither human nor diabolical wisdom could foresee or penetrate; that the defeat of the Israelites, and the death of Saul and his three sons on the following day, were matters which, from their nature, could only be known to God himself; and that no demon or bad spirit could be employed in such a transaction.  <chapter eID="1Sam.28"/> <div eID="gen10552" type="x-p"/>

entries.645cb67935947f90247c0a7d8ffa4005d39940a7: <reference osisRef="1Sam.28.1-1Sam.28.2">1Sa 28:1-2</reference> <div eID="gen4150" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4151" type="x-p"/> “<hi type="italic">In those days</hi>,” i.e., whilst David was living in the land of the Philistines, it came to pass that the Philistines gathered their armies together for a campaign against Israel. And Achish sent word to David that he was to go with him in his army along with his men; and David answered (<reference osisRef="1Sam.28.2">1Sa 28:2</reference>), “<hi type="italic">Thereby</hi> (on this occasion) <hi type="italic">thou shalt learn what thy servant will do</hi>.” This reply was ambiguous. The words “what thy servant will do” contained no distinct promise of faithful assistance in the war with the Israelites, as the expression “<hi type="italic">thy servant</hi>” is only the ordinary periphrasis for “<hi type="italic">I</hi>” in conversation with a superior. And there is just as little ground for inferring from <reference osisRef="1Sam.29.8">1Sa 29:8</reference> that David was disposed to help the Philistines against Saul and the Israelites; for, as Calovius has observed, even there he gives no such promise, but “merely asks for information, that he may discover the king’s intentions and feelings concerning him: he simply protests that he has done nothing to prevent his placing confidence in him, or to cause him to shut him out of the battle.” Judging from his previous acts, it would necessarily have been against his conscience to fight against his own people. Nevertheless, in the situation in which he was placed he did not venture to give a distinct refusal to the summons of the king. He therefore gave an ambiguous answer, in the hope that God would show him a way out of this conflict between his inmost conviction and his duty to obey the Philistian king. He had no doubt prayed earnestly for this in his heart. And the faithful God helped His servant: first of all by the fact that Achish accepted his indefinite declaration as a promise of unconditional fidelity, as his answer “<hi type="italic">so</hi> (לכן, <hi type="italic">itaque</hi>, i.e., that being the case, if thy conduct answers to thy promise) “<hi type="italic">I will make thee the keeper of my head</hi>” (i.e., of my person) implies; and still more fully by the fact that the princes of the Philistines overturned the decision of their king (1Sa 29:3.).
entries.4b27e90e93ec3603e586ec3560bb3231a76bb3ab: <reference osisRef="1Sam.28.3">1Sa 28:3</reference> <hi type="italic">Saul with the witch at Endor</hi>. - The invasion of Israel by the Philistines, which brought David into so difficult a situation, drove king Saul to despair, so that in utter helplessness he had recourse to ungodly means of inquiring into the future, which he himself had formerly prohibited, and to his horror had to hear the sentence of his own death. This account is introduced with the remark in <reference osisRef="1Sam.28.3">1Sa 28:3</reference> that Samuel was dead and had been buried at Ramah (cf. <reference osisRef="1Sam.25.1">1Sa 25:1</reference>; וּבעירו, with an explanatory <hi type="italic">vav</hi>, and indeed in his own city), and that Saul had expelled “<hi type="italic">those that had familiar spirits and the wizards out of the land</hi>” (on the terms employed, <hi type="italic">oboth</hi> and <hi type="italic">yiddonim</hi>, see at <reference osisRef="Lev.19.31">Lev 19:31</reference>). He had done this in accordance with the law in <reference osisRef="Lev.19.31">Lev 19:31</reference>; <reference osisRef="Lev.20.27">Lev 20:27</reference>, and Deu 18:10.
entries.9c2579ce8871b67536a3d66f23d1f94b8d4ad833: <reference osisRef="1Sam.28.4-1Sam.28.5">1Sa 28:4-5</reference> <div eID="gen4151" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4152" type="x-p"/> When the Philistines advanced and encamped at <hi type="italic">Shunem</hi>, Saul brought all Israel together and encamped at <hi type="italic">Gilboa</hi>, i.e., upon the mountain of that name on the north-eastern edge of the plain of Jezreel, which slopes off from a height of about 1250 feet into the valley of the Jordan, and is not far from Beisan. On the north of the western extremity of this mountain was <hi type="italic">Shunem</hi>, the present <hi type="italic">Sulem</hi> or <hi type="italic">Solam</hi> (see at <reference osisRef="Josh.19.18">Jos 19:18</reference>); it was hardly two hours distant, so that the camp of the Philistines might be seen from Gilboa. When Saul saw this, he was thrown into such alarm that his heart greatly trembled. As Saul had been more than once victorious in his conflicts with the Philistines, his great fear at the sight of the Philistian army can hardly be attributed to any other cause than the feeling that God had forsaken him, by which he was suddenly overwhelmed.
entries.95079765581ea19e636728d1e68a29e7512434f9: <reference osisRef="1Sam.28.6">1Sa 28:6</reference> <div eID="gen4152" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4153" type="x-p"/> In his anxiety he inquired of the Lord; but the Lord neither answered him by dreams, nor by Urim, nor by prophets, that is to say, not by any of the three media by which He was accustomed to make known His will to Israel. בּיהוה שׁאל is the term usually employed to signify inquiring the will and counsel of God through the Urim and Thummim of the high priest (see at Jdg 1:1); and this is the case here, with the simple difference that here the other means of inquiring the counsel of God are also included. On dreams, see at Num 12:6. According to Num 27:21, <hi type="italic">Urim</hi> denotes divine revelation through the high priest <hi type="italic">by means of the ephod</hi>. But the high priest Abiathar had been with the ephod in David’s camp ever since the murder of the priests at Nob (1Sa 22:20., <reference osisRef="1Sam.23.6">1Sa 23:6</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Sam.30.7">1Sa 30:7</reference>). How then could Saul inquire of God through the Urim? This question, which was very copiously discussed by the earlier commentators, and handled in different ways, may be decided very simply on the supposition, that after the death of Ahimelech and the flight of his son, another high priest had been appointed at the tabernacle, and another ephod made for him, with the <hi type="italic">choshen</hi> or breastplate, and the Urim and Thummim. It is no proof to the contrary that there is nothing said about this. We have no continuous history of the worship at the tabernacle, but only occasional notices. And from these it is perfectly clear that the public worship at the tabernacle was not suspended on the murder of the priests, but was continued still. For in the first years of David’s reign we find the tabernacle at Gibeon, and Zadok the son of Ahitub, of the line of Eleazar, officiating there as high priest (<reference osisRef="1Chr.16.39">1Ch 16:39</reference>, compared with <reference osisRef="1Chr.6.8">1Ch 6:8</reference> and <reference osisRef="1Chr.6.53">1Ch 6:53</reference>); from which it follows with certainty, that after the destruction of Nob by Saul the tabernacle was removed to Gibeon, and the worship of the congregation continued there. From this we may also explain in a very simple manner the repeated allusions to two high priests in David’s time (<reference osisRef="2Sam.18.17">2Sa 18:17</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Sam.15.24">2Sa 15:24</reference>, <reference osisRef="2Sam.15.29">2Sa 15:29</reference>, <reference osisRef="2Sam.15.35">2Sa 15:35</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Chr.15.11">1Ch 15:11</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Chr.18.16">1Ch 18:16</reference>). The reason why the Lord did not answer Saul is to be sought for in the wickedness of Saul, which rendered him utterly unworthy to find favour with God.
entries.f19bbcaa911f5634aa08dbd130387acf36ac20af: <reference osisRef="1Sam.28.7-1Sam.28.14">1Sa 28:7-14</reference> <div eID="gen4153" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4154" type="x-p"/> Instead of recognising this, however, and searching his own heart, Saul attempted to obtain a revelation of the future in ungodly ways. He commanded his servants (<reference osisRef="1Sam.28.7">1Sa 28:7</reference>) to seek for a woman that had a familiar spirit. <hi type="italic">Baalath-ob</hi>: the mistress (or possessor) of a conjuring spirit, i.e., of a spirit with which the dead were conjured up, for the purpose of making inquiry concerning the future (see at <reference osisRef="Lev.19.31">Lev 19:31</reference>). There was a woman of this kind at <hi type="italic">Endor</hi>, which still exists as a village under the old name upon the northern shoulder of the <hi type="italic">Duhy</hi> or Little Hermon (see at <reference osisRef="Josh.17.11">Jos 17:11</reference>), and therefore only two German (ten English) miles from the Israelitish camp at Gilboa.
entries.fce4f3843e0921aebfcc5d1fdd563735875b71e7: <reference osisRef="1Sam.28.15-1Sam.28.17">1Sa 28:15-17</reference> <div eID="gen4160" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4161" type="x-p"/> Then Samuel said, “<hi type="italic">Why hast thou disturbed me</hi> (sc., from my rest in Hades; cf. <reference osisRef="Isa.14.9">Isa 14:9</reference>), <hi type="italic">to bring me up?</hi>” It follows, no doubt, from this that Samuel had been disturbed from his rest by Saul; but whether this had been effected by the conjuring arts of the witch, or by a miracle of God himself, is left undecided. Saul replied, “<hi type="italic">I am sore oppressed, for the Philistines fight against me, and God has departed from me, and answers me no more, either by prophets or by dreams; then I had thee called</hi> (on the intensified form ואקראה, vid., <hi type="italic">Ewald</hi>, §228, <hi type="italic">c</hi>.), <hi type="italic">to make known to me what I am to do</hi>.” The omission of any reference to the Urim is probably to be interpreted very simply from the brevity of the account, and not from the fact that Saul shrank from speaking about the oracle of the high priest, on account of the massacre of the priests which had taken place by his command. There is a contradiction, however, in Saul’s reply: for if God had forsaken him, he could not expect any answer from Him; and if God did not reply to his inquiry through the regularly appointed media of His revelation, how could he hope to obtain any divine revelation through the help of a witch? “When living prophets gave no answer, he thought that a dead one might be called up, as if a dead one were less dependent upon God than the living, or that, even in opposition to the will of God, he might reply through the arts of a conjuring woman. Truly, if he perceived that God was hostile to him, he ought to have been all the more afraid, lest His enmity should be increased by his breach of His laws. But fear and superstition never reason” (Clericus). Samuel points out this contradiction (<reference osisRef="1Sam.28.16">1Sa 28:16</reference>): “<hi type="italic">Why dost thou ask me, since Jehovah hath departed from thee, and is become thine enemy?</hi>” The meaning is: How canst thou expect an answer under these circumstances from me, the prophet of Jehovah? ערך, from ער, signifies an enemy here (from עיר, <hi type="italic">fervour</hi>); and this meaning is confirmed by <reference osisRef="Ps.139.20">Psa 139:20</reference> and <reference osisRef="Dan.4.16">Dan 4:16</reference> (Chald.). There is all the less ground for any critical objection to the reading, as the Chaldee and Vulgate give a periphrastic rendering of “enemy,” whilst the lxx, Syr., and Arab. have merely paraphrased according to conjectures. Samuel then announced his fate (<reference osisRef="1Sam.28.17-1Sam.28.19">1Sa 28:17-19</reference>): “<hi type="italic">Jehovah hath performed for himself, as He spake by me</hi> (לו, for himself, which the lxx and <hi type="italic">Vulg.</hi> have arbitrarily altered into לך, σοί, <hi type="italic">tibi</hi> (to thee), is correctly explained by Seb. Schmidt, 'according to His grace, or to fulfil and prove His truth'); <hi type="italic">and Jehovah hath rent the kingdom out of thy hand, and given it to thy neighbour David</hi>.” The perfects express the purpose of God, which had already been formed, and was now about to be fulfilled.
entries.e8a9be0afb639aeb4731e666fd4e8a8e4d4b38b0: <reference osisRef="1Sam.28.18-1Sam.28.19">1Sa 28:18-19</reference> <div eID="gen4161" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4162" type="x-p"/> The reason for Saul’s rejection is then given, as in <reference osisRef="1Sam.15.23">1Sa 15:23</reference> : “<hi type="italic">Because</hi> (כּאשׁר, according as) <hi type="italic">thou ... hast not executed the fierceness of His anger upon Amalek, therefore hath Jehovah done this thing to thee this day</hi>.” “This thing” is the distress of which Saul had complained, with its consequences. ויתּן, <hi type="italic">that Jehovah may give</hi> (= for He will give) Israel also with thee into the hand of the Philistines. “To-<hi type="italic">morrow wilt thou and thy sons be with me</hi> (i.e. in Sheol, with the dead); <hi type="italic">also the camp of Israel will Jehovah give into the hand of the Philistines</hi>,” i.e., give up to them to plunder. The overthrow of the people was to heighten Saul’s misery, when he saw the people plunged with him into ruin through his sin (<hi type="italic">O. v. Gerlach</hi>). Thus was the last hope taken from Saul. His day of grace was gone, and judgment was now to burst upon him without delay.
entries.4691c53522eb432cdf1b605b509f37a3b3d1a7dc: <reference osisRef="1Sam.28.20">1Sa 28:20</reference> <div eID="gen4162" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4163" type="x-p"/> These words so alarmed him, that he fell his whole length upon the ground; for he had been kneeling hitherto (<reference osisRef="1Sam.28.14">1Sa 28:14</reference>). <hi type="italic">He “fell straightway</hi> (<hi type="italic">lit</hi>. he hastened and fell) <hi type="italic">upon the ground. For he was greatly terrified at the words of Samuel: there was also no strength in him, because he had eaten no food the whole day and the whole night</hi>,” sc., from mental perturbation or inward excitement. Terror and bodily exhaustion caused him to fall powerless to the ground.
entries.8acb76986655c5493e995c8b56725f5bd4d22ec2: <reference osisRef="1Sam.28.21-1Sam.28.22">1Sa 28:21-22</reference> <div eID="gen4163" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4164" type="x-p"/> The woman then came to him and persuaded him to strengthen himself with food for the journey which he had to take. It by no means follows from the expression “<hi type="italic">came unto Saul</hi>,” that the woman was in an adjoining room during the presence of the apparition, and whilst Samuel was speaking, but only that she was standing at some distance off, and came up to him to speak to him when he had fallen fainting to the ground.
